This sounds extreme and I wouldn’t have believed it even a year ago, but we’re starting to see plenty of examples of productivity gains that are an order of magnitude or two above output levels pre-AI. 

With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a relatively new codebase (with some exceptions), a fluency of how to work with multiple agents at once, and a setup that makes it so you can test and deploy with limited friction, outputs on this level feel realistic in coding.  

What’s crazy is this gap doesn’t appear to be diminishing over time. You’d think that we’d see a convergence in the lines because of AI, but it turns out the more depth you had before -and willingness now to take a different approach- gives you crazy leverage. And that is only compounding as the models can take on larger work and harder problems.

Right now this is most pronounced in software engineering for the obvious reasons. But there’s no reason we don’t start to see this in a number of other computer-use-sensitive domains like other scientific fields, AEC, finance, cyber, and more. Going to get quite wild.

The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. 

Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. 

And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. 

Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.

Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.

A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

This Week in the Arena: Open weights, faster image generation, and new #1s.

- @Kimi_Moonshot released the open weights for Kimi K3.1 Pro, which ranks #1 among open models in Agent Arena with +5.3% net improvement.

- Hy4 by @TencentHunyuan debuted as the #1 Chinese model in Agent Arena. With +5.4% net improvement at a $0.57 median cost per task, it also reshaped the Pareto frontier. Its open weights are coming soon.

- Inkling 2 Small by @thinkymachines arrived in Code Arena: WebDev with 1648 pts. Once its weights are released, it would rank #1 among US open models.

- Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash by @GoogleDeepMind debuted at #1 in both Text-to-Video (1541 pts) and Image-to-Video (1502 pts).

- GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst and Flare by @OpenAI arrived in the Arena at almost 2x the speed of their predecessor, GPT Image 2.5. Sunburst (Medium) landed at #2 in Text-to-Image (1409 pts) and #3 in Image Edit (1476 pts).

See more in the full update.

https://t.co/QCAttpKcuw

OpenAI's GPT Image 2.6 takes #1 and #2 on both AA-Image-T2I v2.1 and AA-Image-Editing v2.1. GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare with slightly better quality, and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst takes the top spot with longer generation times

OpenAI released GPT Image 2.6 on November 4 in ChatGPT, Codex and the API. The API offers two models, GPT Image 2.6 Flare and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst, which follow GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst. Both support Text to Image and Image Editing, and add animated GIF and SVG output. OpenAI added a complexity setting to the API, which controls how much the model plans before rendering. We benchmarked both models at max quality, with complexity at its API default of high.

In our testing, GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare while delivering slightly better quality. Its median Text to Image generation time fell from about 55 to 30 seconds, and its editing time fell from about 58 to 32 seconds. GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst goes the other way: it takes longer than GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, at about 2 minutes 15 seconds per image, and takes the #1 spot. Its largest Text to Image gains are in Reasoning, Text Rendering, Lighting and Material, and it is strongest in UIUX Design.

Both models cost $30 per 1M image output tokens, the same as GPT Image 2.5. That is about $0.21 per 1024x1024 image at max quality ($211 per 1k images).

GPT Image 2.6 is available in ChatGPT and Codex across all tiers, and in the OpenAI API.

Congratulations to @OpenAI on the release!
